patient.history_present_illness: A 63-year-old man with known hepatitis C cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma on the liver transplant waiting list was brought to the emergency department by his wife due to three days of progressively worsening confusion. His wife reports that he initially seemed forgetful and was mixing up family members' names, which she attributed to fatigue. By day two, he was sleeping most of the day, becoming difficult to rouse for meals, and had stopped taking his afternoon lactulose dose because he kept forgetting. On the day of presentation, he could not recognize their home and was asking to go back to Mexico (he has lived in the United States for 35 years). He had no witnessed seizures, no falls, no headaches, and no complaints of pain. His wife noted his abdomen appeared more distended than usual and that his urine had been darker over the past two days. She also reported that he had developed a low-grade fever at home (measured 38.2°C) and had complained of mild abdominal discomfort. He has been compliant with his transplant evaluation requirements and had a routine hepatology appointment scheduled for next week. He has been abstinent from alcohol for 8 years and achieved sustained virologic response on hepatitis C treatment. His wife denied any recent medication changes, new supplements, or obvious dietary indiscretions. He had a prior episode of hepatic encephalopathy eighteen months ago that required hospitalization but resolved completely with lactulose and rifaximin intensification.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II-III), hepatitis C cirrhosis with small HCC on transplant list (Child-Pugh B, MELD 16) — precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

differential.key_features: MRI if clinical course atypical or focal deficits develop.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (SBP empiric therapy; AASLD HE; transplant prioritization).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering antibiotics, lactulose, rifaximin, immunosuppression as relevant; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.
Ascitic PMN ≥250 confirms SBP; start ceftriaxone + albumin.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — characterize HE pattern. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Consult hepatology + transplant team — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

optimal_actions.action: Perform a diagnostic paracentesis and send ascitic fluid for cell count with differential, protein and culture, inoculating blood-culture bottles at the bedside
optimal_actions.expected_finding: A polymorphonuclear count at or above 250 cells/mm3 establishes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is a precipitant that must be treated whether or not fever or leucocytosis is present

optimal_actions.action: Send urine for microscopy and culture as part of the infection screen
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pyuria and bacteriuria identify a urinary source; a negative result removes it from the list of precipitants

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Empiric ceftriaxone for SBP; albumin per protocol.
Update transplant team — HE episode affects MELD-Na exception logic.
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Documented overt HE episodes affect transplant prioritization decisions and should be communicated to the transplant team.
